new_statements.quote: Stress is not phonemic in 'Are'are. Lexical stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word and phrasal stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phrase: /'ɾo.to/ 'swim' /ɾo.'to.ha/ 'swimming' /'ma.ne/ 'man' /ma.ne.'ne.na/ 'that man' However there are exceptions. If the final syllable contains a long vowel, it will be stressed: /'ha.na/ 'eat' /ha.'ɾaː/ 'wash' If the antepenultimate syllable contains a long vowel it will be stressed: /'aː.wa.ɾa/ 'ten' /'oː.hi.ja/ 'cradle (baby)' In a disyllabic lexeme or phrase where both syllables contain long vowels or diphthongs, the penultimate syllable is stressed. [...] Function (grammatical) words are normally unstressed.
new_statements.citation: Naitoro, Katerina. 2013. A sketch grammar of 'Are'are: The sound system and morpho-syntax. MA thesis, University of Canterbury. DOI 10.26021/5071.

Lexical stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word and phrasal stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phrase: /'ɾo.to/ 'swim' /ɾo.'to.ha/ 'swimming' /'ma.ne/ 'man' /ma.ne.'ne.na/ 'that man' However there are exceptions. If the final syllable contains a long vowel, it will be stressed: /'ha.na/ 'eat' /ha.'ɾaː/ 'wash' If the antepenultimate syllable contains a long…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (and of the phrase), but a long vowel elsewhere attracts stress: a final long vowel is stressed (ha.'raː 'wash'), an antepenultimate long vowel is stressed ('aː.wa.ra 'ten'); when both syllables of a disyllable are heavy (long vowel or diphthong) the penult wins. Stress is not contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; only 'primary stress' is marked in the phonetic transcriptions (p. 24).
new_statements.exceptions: /iː.'taː/ 'what' has final stress although both syllables are long ('seems to be an exception', p. 24). Function (grammatical) words are normally unstressed and their vowels, especially high vowels, are commonly deleted (pp. 24, 30-31).
new_statements.domain_note: Both word and phrase: lexical stress on the penult of the word, phrasal stress on the penult of the phrase (e.g. [taʔaːn 'mane] 'the males'). Based on the 'middle' dialect (Ta'arutona to Rohinari), main consultant and fieldwork in Hauporo, West 'Are'are; auditory analysis, no instrumental study.
new_statements.identity_note: Naitoro 2013 describes the 'middle' dialect of 'Are'are (Ta'arutona to Rohinari; consultants from Hauporo, West 'Are'are), the language-level languoid area1240; Glottolog lists no dialect glottocodes. Ivens 1929/1932 (not opened) describe the Marau Sound emigrant dialect on Guadalcanal, which Tryon & Hackman 1983 treat as one of seven 'Are'are dialects. Geerts 1970 is based on the Tarapaina (Small Malaita Passage) variety.

sources.note: Sect. 2.2 'Stress', pp. 23-24: stress not phonemic; lexical stress normally on the penultimate syllable of the word and phrasal stress on the penult of the phrase; a long vowel in the final or antepenultimate syllable attracts stress; if both syllables of a disyllable are long/diphthongal the penult is stressed; /iː.'taː/ 'what' is an exception with final stress; function words are normally unstressed and often lose their vowels.

sources.citation: Naitoro, Katerina. 2019. Morphs in search of meaning: Southeast Solomonic transitive morphology in diachronic perspective. PhD thesis, Australian National University. Handle 1885/163714.
sources.note: Comparative-historical morphology; no 'Are'are stress rule. pp. 219-220: 'The descriptions available for SES languages rarely discuss specifics of stress assignment in verbs with longer suffixes'; cites Ross (pers. comm.) that SES languages have CV syllable structure and unstressed vowels lose little or no quality.

sources.citation: Geerts, P. 1970. 'Āre'āre Dictionary. Pacific Linguistics C-14. Canberra: Australian National University. iv+191 pp.
sources.note: No pronunciation or phonology section; the preface (p. iii) refers the reader to Ivens 1927 (Oroha) for grammar. Only isolated lexical notes inside entries, e.g. 'a'a 'Don't!' (accent on last 'a) vs. exclamation of assent (accent on first 'a), p. 1. Naitoro 2013:3 confirms the dictionary gives no information on pronunciation or the sound system.
